https://www.echo-news.co.uk/news/2629235.text: Ryanair warns of long EES queues at 16 European airports Entry Exit System Ryanair Leisure Travel By Patrick Glover Trending News Reporter Share 0 Comments The EU's Entry/Exit System (EES) continues to cause disruptions. (Image: Getty Images) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Ryanair has warned Brits travelling to Europe this summer to expect "significant" queues at 16 major airports. The warning comes as the European Union's Entry/Exit System (EES) continues to create disruptions, months after its introduction. The EES was first introduced in October last year, before the rollout ramped up on April 10. The new system requires British travellers and other non-EU visitors to provide biometric data, including fingerprints and facial scans, when entering the Schengen Area. The new EES has received significant backlash since its introduction, with it causing long waits for passengers at airports. Some travellers have already experienced waits of up to six hours, and industry experts warn these disruptions could continue for up to two years . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Portugal Travel Advisor | Julia T (@travel_luckk) Major airlines, including Jet2 and Ryanair, have called for the rollout of the new system to be suspended until after the summer to allow for a "smoother airport experience" during peak travel season. CEO of Malta Air, David O’Brien, even threatened to pull all flights to Malta due to the extended wait times caused by the EES at airports. EES to cause long queues at these 16 major airports this summer Brits heading to Europe this summer have been told to expect more delays due to the EES. Ryanair has outlined 16 European Airports where travellers can expect "significant" queues: Tenerife South Palma/Majorca Alicante Malaga Milan Bergamo Krakow Paris Beauvais Lisbon Madrid Lanzarote Milan Malpensa Verona Berlin Cologne Frankfurt Hahn Budapest Chief operations officer at Ryanair, Neal McMahon, said: "Families heading away for a well-earned summer holiday should be thinking about suitcases, suncream and sangria, not standing in passport queues for hours. "The reality is that the EES system isn’t working properly and families are paying the price for a system that does not work months after launch. "Passengers should not be the testing ground for unfished border infrastructure." Mr McMahon has backed calls from EU Member States to extend current EES flexibilities into early 2027. This extension would give airports and border authorities more time to fix malfunctioning kiosks, increase staffing levels, and ensure the system can operate efficiently before full enforcement is introduced. He said: "We support calls from EU Member States to urgently extend the EES flexibilities. "This will give airports and border authorities the time to improve the infrastructure, fix the broken devices and hire more staff so that families can travel through Europe without disruption." Ryanair has advised UK passengers travelling to and from non-Schengen destinations, or transiting through affected European airports, to allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for lengthy waits at passport control. ETIAS launch delayed until 2027 Meanwhile, the launch of the EU's new European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) has been delayed until 2027 . The ETIAS is a pre-authorisation scheme which will apply to UK passport holders and other visa-exempt travellers entering 30 European countries for short stays. Applicants will be required to pay a €20 fee, though travellers under 18 or over 70 will be exempt. The ETIAS was expected to launch later this year, but it has now been delayed until 2027, according to the Financial Times . The decision is due to "technical glitches" and delays with the EES, which only recently came online after being postponed from 2022. EU home affairs commissioner, Magnus Brunner, said the delays were due to "other factors", including insufficient staff or lack of adequate infrastructure. EU-Lisa, the agency responsible for ETIAS, has reportedly acknowledged that "launching it by the end of this year as planned was no longer feasible". The European Commission will set the official launch date only after EU-Lisa confirms the system has been fully tested and is ready. https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-drone-cra.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iccw A Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft came down in a field about 100 meters from a border checkpoint with Romania Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP Advertisement When a drone entered Bulgaria 's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from. Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems. And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged. The Kardam border crossing (pictured here) is close to a Bulgarian compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable." Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident. What is known about the incident? At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania. Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field. In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives." Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged. Drone came down near gas pipeline The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine , and in close proximity to a Romanian station. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov (left, pictured here with Prime Minister Radev) has said Bulgaria needs 'new (anti-drone) systems that need to be bought fast' Image: BGNES This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target. Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low. Wake-up call for Bulgaria Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability. "Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT. While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania , these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach. Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though h e admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country. " Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last met at the NATO summit in Ankara in July Image: BGNES With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Was Russia involved? As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria. According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated. Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals. He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective. The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication. Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash. "The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case. As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine. Bulgaria has declined an invitation from French President Emmanuel Macron (center left) to join the Coalition of the Willing, which last met with Ukrainian representatives in Paris in July (seen here) Image: Tom Nicholson/AFP The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine. Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador. "This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position. A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party. While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy , promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine. Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine , blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing , which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine. "I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here." Share WhatsApp Facebook X Linkedin Reading Time: 4 minutes Yash Fatania In October or November last year, Yash Fatania’s supervisor gave him a hint: he might get the opportunity to work on a satellite the following year. Then, nothing. The idea went quiet until February 2026, when the team finally came together and the possibility suddenly became real. Fatania, an Edith Cowan University engineering graduate , was going to work on hardware that would eventually travel into space. “I felt a mix of things at once, but mostly disbelief,” he tells Indian Link in a candid chat. “I couldn’t believe I would be putting my hands on hardware that was actually going to space.” A few months later, in June, the experience became even more tangible. During Assembly, Integration and Testing (AIT), Fatania signed the satellite himself. “That was the moment it stopped feeling abstract.” (Source: ECU) The satellite Fatania helped integrate alongside fellow ECU student Andrew Burton is scheduled to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in 2027. NO ROOM FOR ERROR Born and raised in Kenya, Fatania is of Indian heritage and has built his engineering career in Australia. Getting his hands on space-bound hardware was the culmination of months of work; this included preparing ECU’s newly opened ISO 6 (Class 1000) cleanroom to meet the standards required for space-related work. The facility would eventually become the setting for Fatania’s experience with the satellite, where he worked alongside professionals from LC60 AI – LatConnect 60 and engineers from Lithuanian small satellite integrator Kongsberg NanoAvionics. The team who built the first satellite for the cleanroom. (Source: ECU) For Fatania, preparing the facility itself offered an early lesson in just how much work happens before a satellite can even be touched. There was extensive documentation to work through, environmental controls to establish, alarms to configure, and strict guidelines to meet. Coordinating between different parties to keep everything moving was another challenge. “At the time, I questioned how much paperwork we had to work through,” Fatania shares. Looking back, however, he sees the documentation as an essential part of the process. Every requirement, from cleanliness and environmental conditions to compliance and certification, mattered. “Space is not easy,” he confesses. “There is no room for error.” THE SKY IS THE LIMIT SPACEX FALCON 9 The months of preparation finally paid off when the first satellite entered the facility. Then came the part Fatania had been waiting for: working directly with the hardware that would eventually travel into orbit. The payload integration was “very intense”. Early in the process, the team encountered a hardware issue that required them to rethink how a component would fit and sit inside the satellite housing. It took several days of analysis and discussion before they found a safe way to package it. (Source: ECU) Later, they encountered a technical issue involving communication between different systems on board. The team spent about three days testing possibilities one at a time before identifying the cause. For Fatania, both incidents reinforced the same lesson: engineering is often about resisting the urge to rush. “Slow down, go back to first principles, and work the problem methodically until it broke.” As the intern in the room, Fatania says the pressure of working on hardware destined for space manifested mainly in the questions he found himself asking. (Source: ECU) There was little tolerance for shortcuts. From gowning up and entering the cleanroom correctly to handling tools and hardware, every step had to be carried out with precision. Yash Fatania “There was no room for compromise anywhere,” he says. Every action was checked, then checked again, then checked a third time before anyone touched the hardware. “You don’t see this level of precision at a mechanic’s garage or a construction site. It is a different standard altogether.” AIMING FOR THE STARS One of the most rewarding moments came when the team encountered an issue involving a connector cable. Rather than immediately testing possible solutions on the physical hardware, Fatania suggested working through the problem in CAD first. The approach meant the team could test a solution virtually before taking any risk with the real hardware. The eventual testing was a collective effort, with the team brainstorming ideas and working through the options together. But for Fatania, being able to contribute to the process and see an idea led to a practical solution was significant. (Source: ECU) Fatania says, “What stood out most was watching basic principles from the classroom get applied practically. Recalling the theory and then seeing it play out in real hardware and real decisions is what made everything click into place. That’s something a lecture or a textbook can only take you halfway toward.” The satellite is part of LC60’s SWIRSAT1 mission, designed to capture high-resolution data on carbon emissions and environmental changes. Before working on SWIRSAT1, Fatania had already been considering whether he might move towards the space industry. But there was another field competing for his attention: aircraft. Now, he finds himself genuinely caught between the two. Yash Fatania “Right now, I’m genuinely torn between the world of spacecraft and the world of aircraft, and I’m still figuring out where I land.” For other young students, his advice is simple: “Be bold. Take risks.” “Don’t let your dream stay a dream. Push boundaries, chase growth and change, and you’ll see it turn into reality right in front of you.” READ ALSO: Astronauts Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore splash back home Like what you read? Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A suspect has been taken into custody, according to the Philadelphia police commissioner. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Philadelphia Man with gun kills one Philadelphia police officer and injures another 10-year police veteran Shane Seiber was killed after responding to a report of a man with a gun Associated Press and Guardian staff Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Philadelphia police officer was fatally shot and another was wounded on Saturday after responding to a report of a man with a gun, authorities said. Shane Seiber, 40, was killed early on Saturday morning in West Philadelphia , according to the city’s police commissioner, Kevin Bethel. Seiber, a 10-year veteran of the Philadelphia police department, and the other officer were transported to the Penn Presbyterian medical center, where the surviving officer underwent surgery. He was listed in stable condition, Bethel said. Bethel also said a suspect was in custody. Citing law enforcements sources, the Philadelphia Inquirer identified that suspect as Eric Lewis. The Inquirer also reported that Lewis, 35, was employed by Philadelphia’s municipal water department. Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, said he ordered flags to fly at half-mast for Seiber. He is survived by his wife and two children: a boy, age seven, and a girl, three. Seiber was at least the 376th Philadelphia police department officer to die in the line of duty since 1851, according to the Officer Down Memorial Page , which honors US law enforcement personnel who died while on the job. He was the 129th of those officers to die from gunfire, the memorial page said.
